newsitem.title: UK: BT says can protect investors from MCI woes.
newsitem.headline: BT says can protect investors from MCI woes.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc said on Monday it could protect its investors if the terms of its troubled $20 billion planned merger with American telephone carrier MCI Communications Corp needed to be renegotiated.
"We believe that we have got the legal protection that we need for our shareholders," a company spokeswoman said.
Confusion has mounted amid speculation that BT may be unable to rejig the deal despite unexpected news last week of much higher-than-expected losses in MCI's expanding local telecoms business.
The news sent both BT's and MCI's shares tumbling and institutions have voiced concerns that at current share prices, BT is overpaying for MCI.
But sources close to MCI, which has a reputation of not shying away from court action, have been quoted as saying that, according to the terms of the original merger, BT cannot reopen talks.

A group of BT and MCI senior executives -- including BT's finance director Robert Brace and both MCI's chief executive Gerald Taylor and chairman Bert Roberts -- left for Washington on Sunday to spearhead a review of MCI's operations and discuss the future of the merger.

BT's chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield is scheduled to join the party later this week. Asked why he was delaying his departure for MCI's headquarters, the BT spokeswoman said: "He has other things to do as well."
She said the review would be completed as speedily as possible but could give no guidelines.
"We are conscious that people are looking for more information and as soon as we have that we can tell them... It will take as long as it takes," she said.

Although MCI told BT in March it expected higher losses than previously forecast because of problems breaking into lucrative local U.S. markets, BT says it was surprised and disappointed by the scale of a profit warning announced at an MCI board meeting last Wednesday.
MCI said it expected $800 million losses this year in its local business -- double previous estimates -- and more next year.
As time drags on, some analysts say the previously slim odds of the merger falling apart completely are rising.

BT stresses, however, that it is committed to its strategy of investing in the U.S. and forming a global telecoms giant so it can sell communications services to high-margin, multinational corporate customers around the world.
